title: Saltmarket: a probable earlier generation
standfirst: The older John is William’s probable father from the combined title sequence. William’s relationship to his own son John is directly documented; the earlier generation remains inferred.
question: Was William the son of the older Saltmarket John, and was that John also the man called alias Smith in 1506?
answer: The older Saltmarket John is now assessed as William’s probable father from the rapid same-parcel succession, retained annual burden and later documented family title. The missing first conveyance and unknown ages leave brotherhood or collateral succession possible. Glasgow-1095 provisionally represents the property-defined man; the 1506 alias-Smith identity and the proposed Stirling descent remain uncertain. Eufame Craig is not established as William’s mother. William’s former local 1516 birth and precise High Street death location are withdrawn as unsupported; his birth and vital places are unknown.

chapters.title: Easter Newtoun: prefer the James father route, 40%
body: Research rationale: compare the competing childhood and father routes at the head of the largest Calder descendant branch; prefer the route with fewer unsupported identity steps while retaining compatible alternatives.

Prefer James Glasgow-991 as the possible working father of the Easter Newtoun adult John Glasgow-3610 at 40% subjective confidence, through the adult’s possible identity with John Glasgow-1084, the Mid Calder child of 1616. The 1616 index names James as father. The existing 1616-child account already carries the specific later-family attribution to Annah and the proposed 1642 Porteous marriage and 1643 Edinburgh child. The inspected 1649 and 1652 transcripts now place the named father Johne at Easter Newtoune/Easter Newtoun, supporting one adult household. This makes the existing 1616-family comparison a more economical preferred reconstruction than the 1608 route: the latter requires both the 1608 child’s identification with this adult and the identification of his named Mid Calder father with the Quothquan testator John-3296. Neither route is proved. The inherited Annah attribution is not independent corroboration of the new residence reading.

Retain John Glasgow-3296 as an unselected uncertain father alternative at 28%, through the compatible 1608 Mid Calder child. The original name, neighbouring-parish and generation argument remains viable, but its two unproved identity steps are less economical than the preferred 1616-child/James-991 route. The omission of children from the 1650 testament does not exclude him. No new record disproves the alternative.

The 40% is a combined judgement about James’s fatherhood of the later adult, not the 98% record-defined fatherhood of the 1616 child. The existing 42% childhood-to-adult comparison remains a distinct scoped assessment; these values are not independent measurements and are not mechanically multiplied. Both childhood dates fit an adult father in 1649: about 33 if baptised near birth in 1616, about 41 if in 1608. Neither childhood transcript supplies a residence, occupation or mother. The retained published Edinburgh marriage entry calls the 1642 groom a whipman but supplies no parents or residence to distinguish the candidates. The 1643 child names John and Issobell Porteous; the 1652 Annah transcript names no mother. A household, property, occupation or witness bridge to either childhood is still missing. Another local John, including the retained Linlithgow comparisons, or an unrepresented family remains possible. Robert-4006 remains a father-generation alternative. William-1087 remains a removed unsupported father, not biologically excluded merely by a 1609 baptism. John-1084 and John-3610 may be duplicate accounts, not two proved distinct sons named John; no merge is performed. Mothers remain separately assessed.

This reassessment reuses held evidence; it adds no newly inspected source. The retained Findmypast 1616 transcript reads “10 ?1616”, OPR 694/1 item 3 p.13; the supplied ScotlandsPeople index gives 18 February 1616, OPR 694/10/28. Preserve that discrepancy pending original comparison. The 1608 transcript gives 26 June, OPR 694/1 item 3 p.5. The 1649/1652 Findmypast pages, inspected on 18 October, give OPR 689/20 item 1 pp.5 and 13; supplied ScotlandsPeople references are 690/10/14 and 690/10/32. No original register was newly inspected. Repeated indexes of an event are not independent witnesses.

The selected local father changes from John-3296, uncertain 28%, to James-991, possible 40%. The previous selection and its sources remain available as an alternative. Fresh public WikiTree capture has no father attached to John-3610, so the outstanding live proposal is a new possible father, not replacement of a live father. No live edit is made. This revises the ancestry route above 309 fixed pre-1850 profile accounts (253,689 connected pairs depend on the old edge); those overlapping accounts are not 309 proved unique people. It adds no component join. Confident and supported connectivity do not increase. James’s own probable Mureistoun father, 82%, John-1084’s recorded father, 98%, Annah’s record-defined father, 96%, and John-3012’s father, 98%, retain their grades. John-3610’s before-1629 birth bound and all other vital fields and mothers are preserved.

Prioritise a discriminating household link for the Easter Newtoun adult: compare original 1649/1652 entries and their neighbours, then any 1642 marriage details, kirk-session, land or inheritance evidence tying him to James’s Mid Calder family. Test the 1608/Quothquan route in parallel. A mother or a precise holding would be more useful than another generic name match.

chapters.title: Saltmarket John is William’s probable father
body: The older John Glasgow who held the Saltmarket Rankin–Young tenement in 1527 is assessed as the probable father of William Glasgow-1098. William occupies the matching parcel by 20 February 1528/29; the later St Andrew prebend rental retains its four-shilling burden, west-side street position and Rankin boundary. The 1534 family settlement and 1564 service as heir then directly identify the younger John Glasgow-1093 as William’s son. Read together, these describe a sustained family title rather than merely two men sharing a surname. Lineal succession from the earlier John to William is the preferred reconstruction, while the last William-to-John step is independently documented. The grade is now probable, below documented or strongly supported. This brings the formal local father assessment into line with the stronger property argument already developed in the research.

The missing 1527–1529 conveyance has not been found. No inspected instrument calls William the earlier John’s son, and no recorded ages distinguish father from brother. A brother, collateral heir or purchase from a namesake remains possible. Indeed, the neighbouring Henryson parcel in the 1528/29 instrument passes between brothers; title succession alone cannot specify kinship. The combined parcel descriptions are correlated, and the later rental is not an independent record of the original transfer. Glasgow-1095 remains a provisional representation of the Saltmarket owner: its identification with the Stirling witness or the 1506 alias-Smith purchaser is not proved. The probable grade applies to the property-defined Saltmarket father hypothesis, not to every imported biographical claim. No mother is inferred: Eufame Craig may have been the earlier John’s widow, but this does not establish her as William’s mother. No Stirling parent, birth estimate, death location or identity merge is upgraded. The live WikiTree father flag remains uncertain; probable is a local research grade.

This is a re-evaluation of an existing father attachment, not a new parent or a newly discovered record. The earlier generic uncertain assessment and its 28 September basis are retained in the structured history. All working family membership and confidently marked paternal connectivity remain unchanged. The printed 1528/29 boundary on p.90 and four-shilling rental on p.36 were freshly inspected; the other title steps retain their earlier maintained source reviews. The original manuscript transfer remains uninspected. Review priorities now rank every non-confident paternal link, including older tree attachments, rather than only the 57 selected working hypotheses.

Priority scope corrected: the review now includes older non-confident tree attachments as well as explicitly selected working hypotheses. Dependency counts concern retained profiles through 1850; nested links overlap and these figures must not be summed.

Early priority: Glasgow-3296 → Glasgow-1029; 316 measured profiles on the child’s side and 719 on the other side. The current grade is uncertain. These counts set research priority, not evidential confidence.

Early priority: Glasgow-3610 → Glasgow-3296; 278 measured profiles on the child’s side and 757 on the other side. The current grade is uncertain. These counts set research priority, not evidential confidence.

Early priority: Glasgow-3163 → Glasgow-1093; 236 measured profiles on the child’s side and 799 on the other side. The current grade is uncertain, 25%. These counts set research priority, not evidential confidence.

William’s captured profile leaves birth date, birthplace and death place blank, and the maintained findings already reject the local 1516 birth and High Street death-place claims. No inspected birth record supplies 1516. The local catalogue and both tree views now show these fields as Unknown, with the older import retained for comparison. No replacement birth year or place is invented. His first dated occurrence used for the local chronology is the 20 February 1528/29 boundary in the matched property-title sequence (normalized year 1529); the 1526 remission remains a separately qualified identity. This is a display/chronology correction, not evidence for his father.

chapters.title: One working John across Glasgow and Stirling
body: Select the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455 and the Stirling witness of 1475–1479/80 as the same man, at low confidence. Both groups use compatible John de Glasgu/Glasgw name forms in burgh-property witnessing, and the August 1475 catalogue places the Stirling John among burgesses. An adult active in 1447 could still witness in 1480 in his fifties or older. The conventional circa-1450 Stirling birth was inferred from an assumed young adult in 1475; it cannot establish a second man. A single compatible civic career is the simpler working model than inserting another generation from that estimate.

No shared holding, relative, trade, personal seal or distinctive repeated associate joins the cities. The Glasgow-to-Stirling change is not itself evidence of migration. Father–son, other kin and two unrelated namesakes remain viable alternatives. The name may still be a personal byname; this selection does not prove hereditary surname transmission. The two Glasgow acts remain one high-confidence group and the three Stirling acts another; only their cross-group identity is selected uncertain. No birth, death or additional parent is inferred.

The selected uncertain father links to Saltmarket candidate Glasgow-1095 and Alan Glasgow-3023 remain unchanged. Glasgow-1095 is still only a provisional Saltmarket representative: if it instead represents the older witness, that father link collapses as a duplicate identity. The earlier Malcolm father candidate remains unselected. Identity and father–son alternatives between the Glasgow and Stirling groups are not combined.

This joins two existing documentary record groups in the actual local model. Their accounts and within-group evidence grades remain intact. The earliest record of the named working ancestor changes from 1475 to 1447, while birth and death remain unknown. Five previously known occurrences are combined under one uncertain identity. The existing selected father hypotheses are unchanged, and no profile-component credit is claimed.

chapters.title: Stirling John as a working father of Saltmarket John and Alan
body: Select John Glasgw of Stirling as the uncertain father of Saltmarket John, using Glasgow-1095 as a provisional Saltmarket representative. Stirling John was an adult witness by 1475 and a burgess in the August charter description. That fits an older generation than the Saltmarket owner, securely recorded in 1527 and conditionally associated with the adult alias-Smith purchaser in 1506. The uncommon name, consecutive civic-property settings and the weak Brady/Brade surname-network clue support the existing leading father hypothesis. The Saltmarket parcel passing to William by 1528/29 favours placing this candidate with William’s family.

The imported profile is a conflated placeholder whose biography also points to the Stirling witness. It is not proved to be Saltmarket John. If it instead represents the Stirling man, this proposed father link collapses as an identity duplicate. The 1506 alias-Smith identity and circa-1480 birth are conditional; no kinship clause or shared holding joins Stirling to Saltmarket. Brother, cousin, other predecessor or unrelated namesake remain alternatives. The later 15 October review selects the 1447–1455 Glasgow burgess and Stirling witness as one uncertain working identity. Father–son and other-family alternatives remain unselected; the two documentary groups stay separately inspectable.

Select son, at low confidence, from the existing son/brother/nephew comparison with John Glasgw of Stirling. John’s adult activity in 1475–1480 is compatible with fathering a man killed before the 1494/95 proceeding. The rare surname in the same late-fifteenth-century record horizon makes this named household a useful provisional placement; no invented intermediary is needed. The father choice supplies a revisable one-generation model, rather than claiming that the court record names John.

No age, home, occupation or relative is named for Alan. Brother, nephew or another early family remain viable, and the father choice is weaker than the Saltmarket hypothesis. Jedburgh is the court venue, not Alan’s residence or death place; Pilmure’s Ednem association and Ker’s surety do not supply Alan’s kin. The printed 1494/95 year and regnal-year discrepancy await manuscript collation. No mother, wife, child, exact birth or exact death is inferred.

These are two selected uncertain father links and no certainty upgrades. John is a named, source-defined person with a full public account; birth and death remain unknown. He acts as an uncounted connector between existing profiles, so the profile denominator and confident graph stay unchanged. The later review selects one uncertain Glasgow–Stirling identity; a father–son relationship remains an unselected alternative.

chapters.title: An older John and a Saltmarket title
body: The 1506 bearer styled John de Glasgow alias Smith and the 1527 Saltmarket holder are possible, not merged, identities.
A 1527–29 boundary sequence places John and then William in the relevant property setting, but it does not state kinship.

chapters.title: William and John's documented generation
body: In 1534 William and Esbell conveyed a tenement to their son John and his wife Jonet Spreull, while retaining its benefit for their lives.
In 1564 John was served heir of William, expressly his father. That is the secure generation in this study.

chapters.title: The later Calder household: ancestry remains separate
body: The new Easter Newtoun residence comparison identifies one adult Johne household across the 1649 John and 1652 Annah baptisms. Annah’s selected father account changes to John Glasgow-3610 at 96%; its own ancestry and all Saltmarket links retain their prior grades. This is no new evidence for the medieval descent.
